slides.title: From World War II to Sand War
slides.body: World War II weakened Europe's colonial empires and accelerated independence across Africa. Algeria and Morocco inherited borders drawn under colonial rule, but disagreed over where sovereignty should lie in the Sahara. Those unresolved territorial claims erupted into the Sand War soon after Algerian independence.

slides.title: Sand War
slides.body:
The Sand War was a border conflict between Algeria and Morocco fought from September 25 to October 30, 1963, although a formal peace treaty was not signed until February 20, 1964. It resulted largely from the Moroccan government's claim to portions of Algeria's Tindouf and Béchar provinces. The Sand War led to heightened tensions between the two countries for several decades. From a French and European diplomatic point of view, the Sand War showed how quickly post-colonial borders in North Africa could become militarized after independence.

Why It Matters: Sand War should be understood through the decisions it forced on France / regional diplomacy. It mattered because France had just left Algeria, yet the regional order it helped create remained fragile and contested. In the wider arc of the war, this event changed calculations about security, legitimacy, escalation, or withdrawal.

slides.title: War Summary: Sand War
slides.cap: The end and legacy of the Sand War
slides.body: Regional mediation stopped the fighting without fully resolving the border dispute. The conflict left a lasting rivalry between Algeria and Morocco.
